title: Condemned to Be Free
objective: After this level you can explain Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence and his idea of bad faith, using his café waiter who plays at being a waiter.
summary: Sartre held that for humans existence precedes essence, so we are condemned to be free and denying it is bad faith; Merleau-Ponty stressed situated freedom.

cards.headline: A paper-knife knows what it’s for. Do you?
cards.body: Before a paper-knife is made, its maker already has its purpose in mind. Jean-Paul Sartre argued that you are the one thing that doesn’t work that way.

cards.headline: Objects: essence first
cards.body: Towards the end of 1945, many thousands of Parisians packed into Sartre’s lecture Existentialism is a Humanism, a popular version of his Being and Nothingness (1943). He began with a paper-knife. Its maker had a conception of what it is and what it’s for before it existed. For manufactured things, Sartre said, essence comes before existence.

cards.headline: You: existence first
cards.body: Humans are different, Sartre argued: “existence precedes essence.” You first exist, turn up in the world, and only afterwards define yourself. No pre-given human nature decides who you’ll be. That’s why he called us “condemned to be free”: condemned because we didn’t create ourselves, free because we are still responsible for everything we do.

cards.headline: The waiter who plays a waiter
cards.body: Pretending you aren’t free is what Sartre called bad faith. His best-known example, in Being and Nothingness, is a café waiter whose movements are a little too precise, a little too waiterly. He’s playing at being a waiter, as if the role decided what he does. It doesn’t. He does, every moment, and some part of him knows it.

cards.headline: Free, but somewhere
cards.body: Critics found this freedom too radical. Maurice Merleau-Ponty argued that our options are already embedded in a social and historical situation “before any personal decision has been made”. As he put it: “We choose the world, and the world chooses us.” Sartre himself later called radical, unconditioned freedom “nonsense”: freedom is always freedom-in-situation.

cards.headline: Condemned to Be Free: the big picture
learned: Bad faith: the waiter playing a waiter
Merleau-Ponty: the world chooses us too

questions.prompt: Who is Sartre’s best-known example of bad faith?

options.label: An artisan making a paper-knife
options.rationale: The paper-knife shows essence before existence.

options.label: A café waiter playing a waiter
A soldier just following orders
options.rationale: His example is a café waiter.

questions.explanation: Sartre’s waiter acts as if his role fixed what he does, denying his own freedom.

questions.prompt: Why did Sartre say humans are “condemned to be free”?

options.label: Society forbids us from choosing for ourselves
Our fixed nature makes every choice for us
We didn’t make ourselves, yet answer for all we do
Freedom is a punishment handed out by the state
options.rationale: The condemnation is our situation, not a sentence.

questions.explanation: We didn’t make ourselves, but with no pre-given nature to hide behind, we are responsible for everything we do.

questions.prompt: In Level 5, a statue’s final cause is what it’s made for. Why does Sartre say a person, unlike a paper-knife, has no such purpose set in advance?

options.label: A person is designed by an artisan first
A person has a final cause but no material cause
options.rationale: Sartre’s point is about essence, not matter.

options.label: A person’s shape is poured like bronze
options.rationale: That describes the statue’s formal cause.

options.label: A person exists first and defines themselves afterwards

questions.explanation: The paper-knife’s purpose exists before it does; a person, Sartre says, exists first and only then defines what they are for.
